cues.text:
On April 4, 1865, an unusual machine began
operating on the eastern edge of London.

At Crossness pumping station,
steam-powered pumps lifted

the city's sewage into
a covered reservoir.
But it wasn't released straight away.

The sewage was held there until the
Thames began to flow out with the tide.

Only then was it
discharged into the river.

This was the southern end of
London's new sewer system.

Across the river, the northern
branch led to Barking Creek.

To understand why London built these
two routes, yet still dumped its waste

into the Thames, we need to go back to
the problem they were supposed to solve.

In the middle of the nineteenth century,
London's sewers emptied waste directly
into the Thames.

The sewage disappeared from sight,
but it remained in the river
flowing through the capital.
And the Thames was a tidal river.
Its current could change direction.

During parliamentary debates in July 1858,
no one could identify a discharge point

where they could be certain the
pollution would never flow back.

Simply carrying sewage beyond
the city wasn't enough.

London also had to decide where that
sewage would enter the water again.

That summer, intense heat and low water
levels made the smell from the polluted
riverbanks unbearable.

The stench reached the Houses of
Parliament in Westminster, disrupting
the work of lawmakers.

Plans for intercepting sewers,
large pipes designed to collect

and redirect the city's waste,
had been discussed before.

The Great Stink made
their construction urgent.

But the smell couldn't answer one
crucial question: where should those new
sewers end?

On July 22, Parliament
debated two options.

One was to discharge the
sewage near Barking Creek.

The other was to carry it
farther downstream, to Sea Reach.

The longer route meant
building more infrastructure.

The shorter route left an unresolved
question about how the sewage
would behave in a tidal river.

During the same debate, a representative
from Woolwich said his district

was already suffering
from London's sewage.

Others challenged that claim,
pointing out that Woolwich
discharged sewage of its own.

The debate did not establish that London's
sewage had caused the reported harm.
The issue remained disputed.

On August 2, Parliament ordered the
Metropolitan Board of Works, the authority

responsible for major public
works in London, to begin
the necessary construction.

The goal was to prevent the capital's
sewage from entering the Thames

within the metropolitan area,
as far as reasonably practical.

But the law did not specify
a single discharge point.
That decision was left to the board.
Soon, it settled on two routes.

The northern sewers would
lead to Barking Creek.

The southern sewers would
lead to Crossness Point.

Sea Reach, the more distant option
discussed in Parliament, was not chosen
for the original system.

In 1859, construction began
on the southern sewers
and Crossness pumping station.

There, steam-powered pumps would lift
the sewage into a covered reservoir.

The waste would be held until the tide was
going out, then released into the river.
Crossness opened in 1865.

Meanwhile, the northern
network continued to develop.

Its Abbey Mills pumping
station was completed by 1868.

And by around 1875, the northern
and southern branches were operating
together as one system.
So London finally had its answer.

Sewage from the north
went to Barking Creek.

Sewage from the south
went to Crossness Point.

The new sewers carried intercepted
waste away from the centre of London.

At Crossness, the reservoir also made it
possible to wait for the outgoing tide
before releasing it.
But there was one major limitation.

The original system did not clean
the sewage before discharging it.
The waste still entered the Thames.
It was simply released farther downstream.

London had changed the route its
sewage travelled and, at Crossness,
the timing of its release.

But it had not turned
sewage into clean water.
